title: Both sides agree the honor of saints is not of one species with divine worship
source_text: LII. Praeterea inde patet Scholae Romanae Doctores, cum Reformatis agnoscere cultum qui Sanctis hominibus & Angelis debetur, non sub eodem genere univoco cum divino cultu contineri; ac proinde non esse ejusdem cum illo speciei: nec cultum istum Religiosum esse, proprie & stricte loquendo: sed solum latiori quadam & minus propria significatione: juxta quam cultum qui Sanctis debetur religiosum dici posse expresse admittunt inter Reformatos insignes Theologi.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover it is evident from this that the Doctors of the Roman School, with the Reformed, acknowledge that the worship which is owed to holy men and Angels is not contained under the same univocal genus with divine worship; and therefore is not of the same species with it: nor is that worship Religious, properly and strictly speaking: but only in a certain broader and less proper signification: according to which notable Theologians among the Reformed expressly admit that the worship owed to the Saints can be called religious.
pass_b_english: It is also clear from this that the teachers of the Roman school agree with the Reformed that the honor owed to holy men and angels does not fall under one univocal genus with divine worship, and so is not of the same species. Nor is that honor religious in the proper and strict sense, but only in a broader and less proper sense. In that sense, eminent theologians among the Reformed expressly allow that the honor owed to the saints may be called religious.

lemmas.gloss: in a broader and less proper signification

choices.why: A scholastic term of art; keeping 'univocal' preserves the precise logical claim.
